flashcards.front: Is the Messages API stateful?
flashcards.back: No. Every request must include all the conversation context you want Claude to see. (Beta message threads can hold a conversation server-side, expiring 5 minutes after the last request.)

flashcards.front: Streaming event that carries the final stop_reason?
flashcards.back: `message_delta`.

flashcards.front: Order of streaming events?
flashcards.back: message_start → content_block_start → content_block_delta… → content_block_stop → message_delta → message_stop (plus ping/error).

flashcards.front: Delta type for streamed tool input?
flashcards.back: `input_json_delta` — partial JSON strings to concatenate, then parse at block stop.

flashcards.front: HTTP 429 means… and how to react?
flashcards.back: rate_limit_error. Back off exponentially with jitter, honour retry-after, smooth traffic.

flashcards.front: HTTP 529 means…
flashcards.back: overloaded_error: high traffic across all users. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter; consider a fallback. Mid-stream it arrives as an error event.

flashcards.front: HTTP 400 — retry?
flashcards.back: No. invalid_request_error is a client bug; fix the request.
401 authentication_error (missing, invalid or expired key); 403 permission_error (the key is not allowed to access the resource).

flashcards.front: Why add jitter to backoff?
flashcards.back: To prevent many clients retrying simultaneously (thundering herd).

flashcards.front: Which header should you log for support tickets?
flashcards.back: `request-id` (response header). Error bodies carry `request_id`, and the Python/TypeScript SDKs expose `_request_id`.

flashcards.front: Do the official SDKs retry automatically?
flashcards.back: Yes: connection errors, 429s and 5xx errors, twice by default, with exponential backoff that honours retry-after. Configure via max_retries / maxRetries.

flashcards.front: Content block type for a PDF?
flashcards.back: `document` (base64, URL or file id source).

flashcards.front: How to get verifiable quotes from a document?
flashcards.back: Enable `citations: {enabled: true}` on the document block.

flashcards.front: Where should images go relative to the question?
flashcards.back: Before the question/instructions.

flashcards.front: Why keep the model ID pinned in config?
flashcards.back: Every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot, so behaviour changes only when someone changes the ID. Keep it in one config value per environment and change it deliberately, after evals.

flashcards.front: Where do prompts belong in a mature codebase?
flashcards.back: Versioned artifacts (files in git / prompt registry) with version logged per output.

flashcards.front: Two ways to keep long chat history affordable?
flashcards.back: Sliding window / summarise older turns; prompt-cache the stable prefix.

flashcards.front: What must follow an assistant message containing tool_use?
flashcards.back: A user message whose tool_result blocks (first in content) match every tool_use id.

flashcards.front: Can you lower temperature for consistency on current Claude models?
flashcards.back: No. temperature, top_p and top_k are unsupported on Claude 4.7+ (non-default values return 400) and return 400 on every model under API version 2026-10-21. Use clear prompts, examples and structured outputs instead.

flashcards.front: Good success criteria are…
flashcards.back: Specific and measurable, tied to the use case, e.g. ≥95% field accuracy on a labelled test set, p95 latency < 4 s, cost per document under a set ceiling.

flashcards.front: What happens to a non-streaming request expected to run over 10 minutes?
flashcards.back: The SDK rejects it. Use streaming or the Message Batches API for long requests, and avoid a large max_tokens without streaming.

flashcards.front: HTTP 504 from the Claude API?
flashcards.back: `timeout_error`: the request timed out. Retry with backoff; if it recurs, reduce work per request or stream.

flashcards.front: How should code tell error types apart?
flashcards.back: Catch the SDK's typed exception classes (e.g. anthropic.RateLimitError, anthropic.NotFoundError); don't string-match error messages.

flashcards.front: Batch custom_id: format and purpose?
flashcards.back: Matches ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$. Results arrive in any order, so join each result to its input by custom_id.

flashcards.front: Batch result types, and which are billed?
flashcards.back: succeeded, errored, canceled, expired. Only succeeded is billed.

flashcards.front: Batch timing and economics?
flashcards.back: 50% of normal cost; most finish within 1 hour; a batch expires if not done in 24 hours; results kept 29 days.

flashcards.front: What is not allowed in a batch request?
flashcards.back: stream: true, fast mode (speed), fallbacks, and max_tokens: 0.

flashcards.front: When are batch request params validated?
flashcards.back: Asynchronously, when the batch ends: invalid requests show up as errored results, not as a rejected submission.

flashcards.front: Why must side-effecting tools be idempotent?
flashcards.back: SDK retries (2 by default), your own retries, queue redelivery or a repeated tool call can run the same action twice. Use an idempotency key and check-then-act.

flashcards.front: A good idempotency key for executing a tool call?
flashcards.back: Something stable for that action: the business ID (order, invoice) or the tool_use id of the call being executed, recorded with the side effect.

flashcards.front: stop_reason model_context_window_exceeded?
flashcards.back: Generation stopped because the context window filled. Treat the output as truncated and shrink the context (trim, summarise, compact).

flashcards.front: What is stop_details?
flashcards.back: Extra information on why a response was refused. It is null for every stop_reason except refusal.

flashcards.front: A 429 with no retry-after that keeps failing usually means…
flashcards.back: A tier spend cap was reached. Backoff will not help; the limit or plan has to change.

flashcards.front: What are acceleration limits?
flashcards.back: A sharp ramp-up in your own traffic can trigger 429s. Ramp traffic up gradually.

flashcards.front: Message threads (beta)?
flashcards.back: A server-side conversation store. A thread expires 5 minutes after its last request, so keep your own durable history.

flashcards.front: Compaction API vs context editing?
flashcards.back: Compaction (beta, header compact-2026-09-04) summarises earlier context on demand or at a token threshold; context editing clears old tool results or thinking by rule.

flashcards.front: Where can a role:"system" message appear on newer models?
flashcards.back: Mid-conversation, after a user turn. It does not invalidate the cached prefix. The main system prompt is still the top-level system parameter.

flashcards.front: Stages of an LLM feature life cycle?
flashcards.back: Define criteria → prototype → build evals → iterate → shadow/canary rollout → monitor, feeding failures back into the evals.

flashcards.front: Three things to have before prompt engineering?
flashcards.back: Clear success criteria, a way to test empirically against them, and a first draft prompt.

flashcards.front: A latency or cost criterion is missed. First lever?
flashcards.back: Often a different model or lower effort, rather than more prompt rewording.

flashcards.front: Shadow mode vs canary?
flashcards.back: Shadow: the new version runs on live traffic but its output is not shown. Canary: the new version serves a small share of real users before full rollout.

flashcards.front: What should differ between dev, staging and prod for a Claude app?
flashcards.back: Config only: credentials (from a secrets manager), model ID, limits, prompt version and flags. The code is the same.

flashcards.front: Are usage counts in streaming message_delta events increments?
flashcards.back: No. They are cumulative totals.

flashcards.front: Run Claude Code non-interactively?
flashcards.back: `claude -p "prompt"` (optionally --output-format json).

flashcards.front: Shared vs personal Claude Code settings files?
flashcards.back: `.claude/settings.json` (shared, committed) vs `.claude/settings.local.json` (personal, git-ignored).

flashcards.front: Where do custom slash commands and subagents live?
flashcards.back: Commands: `.claude/commands/<name>.md` or `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (commands are merged into skills). Subagents: `.claude/agents/`. User-level equivalents live under `~/.claude/`.

flashcards.front: Command to bootstrap a CLAUDE.md?
flashcards.back: `/init` — generates a starting CLAUDE.md, or suggests improvements to an existing one.

flashcards.front: In what order does Claude Code evaluate permission rules?
flashcards.back: Deny, then ask, then allow — first match wins, regardless of specificity. An allow rule cannot override a deny.

flashcards.front: Claude Code settings precedence (highest first)?
flashcards.back: Managed > `--settings` CLI > `.claude/settings.local.json` > `.claude/settings.json` > `~/.claude/settings.json`. List settings like `permissions.allow` merge across scopes.

flashcards.front: Does CLAUDE.md enforce rules?
flashcards.back: No. Claude treats it as context, not enforced configuration. To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a PreToolUse hook (or a deny rule).

flashcards.front: What happens to a tool call needing approval in `claude -p` when no mode is set?
flashcards.back: `-p` starts in Manual mode, so the call is denied unless an allow rule, `--permission-mode`, a PermissionRequest hook or `--permission-prompt-tool` approves it.

flashcards.front: What does `claude -p --bare` skip, and why use it?
flashcards.back: Hooks, skills, plugins, MCP, auto memory and CLAUDE.md. Recommended for reproducible scripted/SDK calls; requires an API key or apiKeyHelper.

flashcards.front: Repo has AGENTS.md but no CLAUDE.md. Does Claude Code use it?
flashcards.back: Yes — recent versions read AGENTS.md when no CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md exists in the cwd or above.

flashcards.front: First three things to check when a Claude call misbehaves?
flashcards.back: Error type/message (and request-id), stop_reason, usage — then the exact request sent.

flashcards.front: Common 400 in tool loops?
flashcards.back: A tool_use block whose id has no matching tool_result block immediately after, in the next user message ("tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after").

flashcards.front: Three grading methods for evals?
flashcards.back: Code-based (exact/regex/schema), LLM-as-judge with rubric, human review.

flashcards.front: Which two stop_reason values mean the output was truncated?
flashcards.back: `max_tokens` and `model_context_window_exceeded`.

flashcards.front: How does a refusal show up in the API response?
flashcards.back: HTTP 200 with `stop_reason: "refusal"`; details are in `stop_details`, which is null for every other stop reason.

flashcards.front: usage shows cache_creation_input_tokens = 0 and cache_read_input_tokens = 0. What does it mean?
flashcards.back: Nothing was cached on that request. Check that a cache_control breakpoint actually reaches the API and that the prefix meets the minimum cacheable length. (A prefix that changes every call shows up differently: cache writes every time, but no reads.)

flashcards.front: Agent SDK run ends with subtype error_max_turns. Is `result` available?
flashcards.back: No. `result` is present only on `success`; every subtype still carries total_cost_usd, usage, num_turns and session_id.

flashcards.front: Context window bounds…
flashcards.back: Total input + output tokens in a single request.

flashcards.front: Cheapest/fastest Claude tier and typical uses?
flashcards.back: Haiku: high-volume, latency-sensitive classification, extraction, routing and sub-agents.

flashcards.front: Which model do the docs suggest starting with for most workloads?
flashcards.back: Opus (currently Opus 5.5), then optimize down by lowering effort or moving to a smaller model if evals allow.

flashcards.front: When to choose Fable (the top tier)?
flashcards.back: The most demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks, where capability outweighs higher cost and latency.

flashcards.front: How to choose a model properly?
flashcards.back: Build an eval set from your real prompts, run it across candidate models and effort levels, and pick the cheapest/fastest configuration that meets your success criteria.

flashcards.front: Prompt caching marker?
flashcards.back: `cache_control: {type: 'ephemeral'}` on a content block.

flashcards.front: Order of the cacheable prefix?
flashcards.back: tools → system → messages.

flashcards.front: Default cache lifetime?
flashcards.back: 5 minutes, refreshed free on each hit (an optional 1-hour TTL costs more to write).

flashcards.front: Usage fields confirming cache behaviour?
flashcards.back: `cache_creation_input_tokens` (writes) and `cache_read_input_tokens` (hits).

flashcards.front: Why might a short system prompt never cache?
flashcards.back: It is below the model's minimum cacheable length (512 tokens on the newest models, higher on older ones); shorter prefixes are silently not cached.

flashcards.front: Batch API discount and latency?
flashcards.back: 50% off; asynchronous, most batches finish within an hour, and a batch expires if not done in 24 hours.

flashcards.front: How to estimate input tokens before sending?
flashcards.back: `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` (free, separate rate limits; the count is an estimate).

flashcards.front: Input or output tokens — which cost more?
flashcards.back: Output tokens (several times the input price).

flashcards.front: How do you control reasoning depth on current Claude models?
flashcards.back: `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}` plus `output_config.effort` (low to max). Manual `budget_tokens` thinking returns 400 on Claude 4.7+.

flashcards.front: Thinking + tool use rule?
flashcards.back: Pass thinking blocks back exactly as received in the assistant turn; modified thinking blocks are rejected.

flashcards.front: Knowledge cutoff mitigation?
flashcards.back: Give Claude tools (web search) or retrieval for current information.

flashcards.front: Three hallucination mitigations?
flashcards.back: Allow "I don't know"; extract direct quotes first / verify with citations; restrict answers to provided documents. They reduce, not eliminate, hallucination.

flashcards.front: Valid values of output_config.effort?
flashcards.back: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`. Default is `medium` on Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, `high` on most other models.

flashcards.front: Is effort a token budget?
flashcards.back: No. It is a behavioural signal. `max_tokens` is the hard cap on thinking plus response text, so set it generously at high effort.

flashcards.front: Does a dateless model ID like claude-opus-5-5 float to newer versions?
flashcards.back: No. Every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot, dateless ones included. Upgrade by changing the ID and re-running evals.

flashcards.front: Context window and max output of the current Claude models?
flashcards.back: 1M tokens of context and 128K max output tokens (check the models overview for live specs).

flashcards.front: Why do token counts rise after migrating from a pre-4.7 model?
flashcards.back: The newer tokenizer (introduced with Opus 4.7) produces about 30% more tokens for the same text.

flashcards.front: temperature / top_p / top_k on current models?
flashcards.back: Not supported on Claude 4.7+ (400), and rejected on any model under API version 2026-10-21. Requests sample at defaults.

flashcards.front: Can thinking be turned off on Opus 5.5?
flashcards.back: No. Thinking is always on for Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.x; lower the effort instead. Haiku 5.5 accepts `disabled` at effort high or below.

flashcards.front: Docs' advice: switch model or tune effort first?
flashcards.back: "Tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models."

flashcards.front: Capability-first vs efficiency-first model selection?
flashcards.back: Capability-first: start on Opus, then optimize down (effort or smaller model). Efficiency-first: start on Haiku and upgrade only if evals show it falls short.

flashcards.front: How do you match Message Batches results to inputs?
flashcards.back: By `custom_id`; results can come back in any order.

flashcards.front: Knowledge cutoff of the current Claude models?
flashcards.back: June 2026 (reliable knowledge and training data). Anything later needs tools, retrieval or supplied documents.

flashcards.front: What should replace "think step by step in <thinking> tags" on the newest models?
flashcards.back: Rely on built-in thinking (lower effort if needed). Asking for written-out reasoning can trigger a reasoning_extraction refusal; manual CoT is a fallback when thinking is off.

flashcards.front: Why use XML tags in prompts?
flashcards.back: Clearly separate instructions, data and examples; easier to reference and parse.

flashcards.front: Ideal few-shot example count and quality?
flashcards.back: About 3–5, relevant, diverse, wrapped in <example> tags.

flashcards.front: Long-document prompt layout?
flashcards.back: Documents at the top, instructions/question at the end.

flashcards.front: What is context engineering?
flashcards.back: Curating the smallest set of high-signal tokens (prompt, tools, docs, history, tool results) for each call.

flashcards.front: Strict tool use for structured data — where's the data?
flashcards.back: In the tool_use block's `input` field; strict: true guarantees it matches the input_schema.

flashcards.front: Validation failure on model JSON — next step?
flashcards.back: Retry with the specific validation error included so Claude can correct it.

flashcards.front: Why make schema fields nullable?
flashcards.back: So Claude can report missing data instead of fabricating values.

flashcards.front: What is context rot?
flashcards.back: Recall degrades as the context grows, so context is a finite attention budget even in large windows.

flashcards.front: Just-in-time retrieval in agents?
flashcards.back: Keep lightweight identifiers (paths, queries) in context and load the data with tools only when needed.

flashcards.front: Lightest-touch long-context technique?
flashcards.back: Tool-result clearing: drop old tool results that have already been used.

flashcards.front: What should a sub-agent return to the lead agent?
flashcards.back: A condensed summary (often 1,000–2,000 tokens), not its full working context.

flashcards.front: "Right altitude" for a system prompt?
flashcards.back: Specific enough to guide behaviour, flexible enough to avoid brittle hardcoded if/else logic.

flashcards.front: GA parameter for JSON structured outputs?
flashcards.back: output_config: {format: {type: "json_schema", schema}}; output_format is deprecated.

flashcards.front: Prefill '{' to force JSON on current models?
flashcards.back: Prefill returns 400 from Claude 4.6 onward; use structured outputs instead.

flashcards.front: When is manual chain-of-thought still appropriate?
flashcards.back: As a fallback when thinking is off; otherwise rely on adaptive thinking and effort.

flashcards.front: Structured outputs — when can the response still be non-conforming?
flashcards.back: On a refusal or a max_tokens stop. Check stop_reason before parsing.

flashcards.front: Schema keywords structured outputs doesn't support?
flashcards.back: Recursive schemas, external $ref, numeric constraints (minimum/maximum/multipleOf), string length limits, minItems other than 0/1.

flashcards.front: "CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool" on newer models?
flashcards.back: Tends to over-trigger; write "Use this tool when…" instead.

flashcards.front: What is indirect prompt injection?
flashcards.back: Malicious instructions embedded in content Claude reads (web pages, docs, tool results).

flashcards.front: Strongest prompt-injection control for a tool-using agent?
flashcards.back: Least-privilege tools + code-enforced authorisation + human approval for sensitive actions.

flashcards.front: Where should API keys live?
flashcards.back: Env vars or a secrets manager, server-side only; never in code, repos, front-ends or prompts.

flashcards.front: Leaked API key — immediate action?
flashcards.back: Revoke/rotate it in the Console, then investigate usage.

flashcards.front: Model output into a web page — required step?
flashcards.back: Escape/sanitise it (treat as untrusted input) to prevent XSS.

flashcards.front: PreToolUse hook exit code that blocks?
flashcards.back: Exit code 2 (stderr is fed back to Claude).

flashcards.front: Hooks vs CLAUDE.md instructions?
flashcards.back: Hooks run deterministically whenever their event fires (exit 2 or a deny decision blocks); CLAUDE.md is context the model usually but not always follows.

flashcards.front: Where should untrusted third-party content be placed in a Messages API conversation to reduce indirect injection risk?
flashcards.back: Only in `tool_result` blocks (labelled with its source, ideally JSON-encoded) — never in the system prompt or as plain user text.

flashcards.front: A policy hook exits with code 1. Does it block the tool call?
flashcards.back: No. Only exit code 2 blocks; any other non-zero code is a non-blocking error.

flashcards.front: Are Claude Code Read deny rules a complete defence for secrets like .env?
flashcards.back: No. They stop the Read tool, not arbitrary subprocesses; use the sandbox for OS-level enforcement.

flashcards.front: Preferred credential approach for production / CI workloads calling the Claude API?
flashcards.back: Short-lived tokens via Workload Identity Federation, or service account keys — not a personal long-lived key.

flashcards.front: When is `bypassPermissions` mode acceptable in Claude Code?
flashcards.back: Only in isolated containers or VMs; admins can disable it via managed settings.

flashcards.front: Your harmlessness-screening call itself returns a refusal. How should you treat it?
flashcards.back: As a harmful verdict — fail closed.

flashcards.front: Three fields of a client tool definition?
flashcards.back: name, description, input_schema (JSON Schema).

flashcards.front: Most important factor in tool selection accuracy?
flashcards.back: A detailed tool description: what it does, when to use it, params, returns, limitations.

flashcards.front: How do you report a tool failure to Claude?
flashcards.back: tool_result with `is_error: true` and an actionable error message.

flashcards.front: tool_choice options?
flashcards.back: auto (default with tools), any, tool (specific name), none (default without tools). any/tool are rejected on some current models.

flashcards.front: How do you get a guaranteed schema-valid tool call on a model that rejects forced tool_choice?
flashcards.back: Use `tool_choice: auto` with `strict: true` on the tool, or use structured outputs for plain JSON. `{type:'tool', name}` forcing returns 400 on models such as Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5.

flashcards.front: Parallel tool calls — how to return results?
flashcards.back: All tool_result blocks together in one user message.

flashcards.front: How to disable parallel tool use?
flashcards.back: `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` in tool_choice (at most one tool per turn).

flashcards.front: MCP: tools vs resources vs prompts control?
flashcards.back: Tools: model-controlled. Resources: application-controlled. Prompts: user-controlled.

flashcards.front: Two main MCP transports?
flashcards.back: stdio (local subprocess, typically one client) and Streamable HTTP (remote, many clients; HTTP POST plus optional SSE).

flashcards.front: Why never print to stdout in a stdio MCP server?
flashcards.back: stdout carries the JSON-RPC protocol; logs corrupt it. Log to stderr.

flashcards.front: Tool to test an MCP server without a model?
flashcards.back: MCP Inspector (`npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector`).

flashcards.front: Python MCP SDK 2.x high-level server class?
flashcards.back: `MCPServer` (`from mcp.server import MCPServer`) with `@mcp.tool()` decorators; older tutorials used `FastMCP`.

flashcards.front: Add an MCP server to Claude Code?
flashcards.back: `claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>` for remote, `claude mcp add <name> -- <cmd>` for stdio, or a project `.mcp.json`.

flashcards.front: Why keep the toolset small and non-overlapping?
flashcards.back: Tool definitions cost tokens and ambiguous overlap causes wrong tool selection.

flashcards.front: Where do text blocks go relative to tool_result blocks in a user message?
flashcards.back: After them. tool_result blocks come first; text before them returns 400.

flashcards.front: What does `strict: true` on a tool definition guarantee?
flashcards.back: Schema-valid tool names and inputs (grammar-constrained).

flashcards.front: What is `input_examples` on a tool and its main constraint?
flashcards.back: Sample inputs that show Claude how to call the tool. They must validate against input_schema (else 400) and add tokens.

flashcards.front: Which MCP features are deprecated in the 2026-07-28 spec, and the replacements?
flashcards.back: Sampling (call LLM APIs directly), roots (pass paths via params/config), logging (stderr or OpenTelemetry).

flashcards.front: TypeScript MCP server package and stdio helper (current SDK)?
flashcards.back: `@modelcontextprotocol/server` with `McpServer`, `registerTool`, and `serveStdio` from `@modelcontextprotocol/server/stdio`.

flashcards.front: Claude Code: are custom slash commands still separate from skills?
flashcards.back: No. Commands are merged into skills; `.claude/commands/x.md` and `.claude/skills/x/SKILL.md` both create `/x`.

flashcards.front: Skill frontmatter to make a skill manual-only?
flashcards.back: `disable-model-invocation: true` (only a user's `/name` runs it). `user-invocable: false` is the opposite: Claude-only.

flashcards.front: Subagent definition: required fields and what happens if `tools` is omitted?
flashcards.back: Only `name` and `description` are required. Omitting `tools` inherits all tools available to subagents.

flashcards.front: How does Claude decide to delegate to a subagent?
flashcards.back: From the subagent's `description`; wording like "use proactively" encourages automatic delegation.

flashcards.front: How much of a skill is in context before it's invoked?
flashcards.back: Only its description; the SKILL.md body loads on invocation.

flashcards.front: Elicitation: how should an MCP server collect an API key from the user?
flashcards.back: URL mode, so the secret never passes through the client or the model. Form mode must not collect passwords, keys or tokens.

questions.stem: According to Anthropic's guidance on building effective agents, what distinguishes an agent from a workflow?
options: In a workflow, LLMs and tools follow predefined code paths; an agent dynamically directs its own process and tool use.
Agents always use multiple models.
Workflows can't use the Claude API.
Agents use tools; workflows never do.
questions.explanation: The key difference is who controls the control flow: your code (workflow) or the model (agent). That is why workflows are more predictable and testable, while agents suit open-ended problems where the steps can't be known in advance.
rationales: Workflows are built on the API.

questions.stem: A team must turn a product spec into marketing copy, check it against brand rules, then translate it into French. Steps are always the same. Which pattern fits best?
options: Autonomous agent with a planning tool
Voting parallelization
Orchestrator-workers
Prompt chaining with an optional programmatic check between steps
questions.explanation: Fixed, sequential steps are the textbook prompt-chaining case; gates between steps catch problems early. An autonomous agent or orchestrator would add cost and unpredictability for no benefit.
rationales: Unnecessary autonomy adds cost and unpredictability.
Voting runs the same task multiple times.

questions.stem: Incoming support messages vary: password resets (simple), billing disputes (moderate), and complex technical bugs. You want to optimise cost without hurting quality on hard cases. Which pattern?
options: Sectioning parallelization.
Prompt chaining with a fixed 5-step pipeline.
Routing: a classifier sends each message to a specialised prompt/model (e.g. smaller model for simple, larger for complex).
Evaluator-optimizer on every message.
questions.explanation: Routing separates input categories so each gets an appropriate prompt and model. Easy categories can go to a smaller, cheaper model while hard ones get a larger model.
rationales: For splitting one task into independent parts.

questions.stem: A coding assistant must make changes across an unknown number of files depending on the request; the files and subtasks can't be known ahead of time. Which pattern fits?
options: Single call with a large context
Prompt chaining
Routing
Orchestrator-workers
questions.explanation: Orchestrator-workers lets a lead model decompose the task dynamically and delegate subtasks to workers. Unlike prompt chaining, the steps are not fixed in code; the orchestrator decides them per request and synthesises the workers' results.
rationales: Routing picks one path; it doesn't decompose.

questions.stem: When is the evaluator-optimizer pattern most appropriate?
options: When there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative feedback measurably improves the output (e.g. literary translation with nuance).
When the task needs the lowest possible latency.
When subtasks are independent.
When the input must be classified.
questions.explanation: Evaluator-optimizer loops generation and critique; it pays off when quality criteria are clear and refinement helps. The extra generate-critique iterations add latency and cost, so they must buy measurable quality.

questions.stem: A content moderation system runs the same 'is this content harmful?' prompt three times with different framings and flags content if two of three say yes. Which pattern is this?
options: Sectioning
Voting (parallelization)
Routing
Prompt chaining
questions.explanation: Voting runs the same task multiple times to get diverse outputs and aggregate them for higher confidence. Sectioning, by contrast, splits a task into different independent subtasks.

options: max_tokens is too small for agents.
It should use streaming.
It terminates on text content instead of stop_reason, never appends the assistant response to msgs, and splits parallel results into separate messages.
tools must be passed only on the first call.
questions.explanation: The loop should branch on stop_reason: continue while it is 'tool_use', and handle end_turn, max_tokens, refusal and the rest explicitly. Each assistant turn (including its tool_use blocks) must be appended to history, and all tool_result blocks for that turn returned together in one user message.
rationales: 1024 may be fine; not the main bug.
Tools must be passed on every request because the API is stateless.

questions.stem: Which safeguards are appropriate for an autonomous agent that can modify production data? (Select three.)
options: Human approval before irreversible actions
Running with all permissions to avoid interruptions
Logging the agent's actions and reasoning for audit
A maximum number of turns or budget as a backstop
questions.explanation: Iteration/budget caps, human checkpoints for high-impact actions and transparent logging are core agent guardrails. Running with every permission removes the very checkpoints that limit damage from compounding errors.

questions.stem: A developer wants to build a custom agent that reads files, edits code, runs shell commands and manages context compaction, without implementing the agent loop from scratch. What should they use?
options: The Claude Agent SDK
The token counting endpoint
A vector database
The Message Batches API
questions.explanation: The Agent SDK exposes the same loop, tools, context management and permission system that power Claude Code. Using it avoids re-implementing the loop, file tools and compaction yourself.

questions.stem: In the Claude Agent SDK, an agent should only search and read a codebase and must never modify files or run shell commands. Which configuration actually enforces that?
options: Tell it in the system prompt not to edit files.
List Read, Grep and Glob in allowed_tools and nothing else.
Put Write, Edit and Bash in disallowed_tools (optionally also auto-approving Read, Grep and Glob via allowed_tools).
Set max_turns to 1.
questions.explanation: In the Agent SDK, allowed_tools only auto-approves the listed tools; unlisted tools remain available and fall through to the permission mode. disallowed_tools blocks tools regardless of other settings, so it is the enforcement mechanism. Capability limits belong in configuration, not prompt text.
rationales: Prompt-only restrictions can be ignored or overridden by injected content.
Tempting, but allowed_tools pre-approves; it does not remove the other tools.

questions.stem: Which Agent SDK interface is best for a multi-turn interactive session where the user sends follow-up messages to the same agent?
options: messages.batches.create()
query()
ClaudeSDKClient
count_tokens()
questions.explanation: query() is a one-shot async iterator; ClaudeSDKClient maintains a session for interactive, multi-turn conversations. The client keeps the conversation state across turns so follow-ups share context.

questions.stem: A team built a three-agent framework (planner, executor, critic) for a task that a single prompt with two examples already solves at 97% accuracy. What does Anthropic's guidance suggest?
options: Switch to Opus for every agent.
Keep the framework; more agents are more robust.
Add a fourth agent for safety.
Prefer the simplest solution that meets requirements; add agentic complexity only when it measurably improves outcomes.
questions.explanation: Agentic systems trade latency and cost for performance. If a simple prompt meets the bar, it's the better design.
rationales: More components add cost, latency and failure modes.

questions.stem: An agent's tool requires file paths. It keeps failing after changing directories because it passes relative paths. Which 'agent-computer interface' improvement best addresses this?
options: Change the tool to require absolute paths and state that clearly in the description (poka-yoke the interface).
Increase max_turns.
Use a larger model.
Add a retry loop around the tool.
questions.explanation: Designing tool parameters so mistakes are hard to make (and documenting them) is more effective than retries or bigger models. The guidance calls this poka-yoke: change the arguments so mistakes are harder to make.
rationales: More turns doesn't fix the cause.
A bigger model may still make the error.

questions.stem: The bot's loop logs a response with HTTP status 200, stop_reason "refusal" and a populated stop_details field. The current code shows the (empty) text to the user as if it were a normal answer. What is the best fix?
options: Treat any HTTP 200 as success and retry only on 4xx/5xx errors.
Detect stop_reason "refusal" in the loop, read stop_details, and route to a fallback (for example a retry on a fallback model or a safe canned reply).
Retry the identical request in a loop until the stop_reason changes.
Lower the temperature so the model refuses less often.
questions.explanation: Refusals arrive as HTTP 200, so status-code checks alone miss them. The stop-reasons guidance is to read stop_details and fall back, for example retrying on a fallback model. Sampling parameters are not supported on current models and are not a refusal control.
rationales: A refusal is itself HTTP 200, so this misses it.
Blind identical retries waste spend and may never succeed.
Temperature is rejected on current models and does not address refusals.

questions.stem: An agent loop that uses a server-side tool receives stop_reason "pause_turn". What should the loop do?
options: Treat it as end_turn and return whatever text is present.
Execute the tool locally and send a tool_result.
Send the assistant content back as-is in a follow-up request (including the container id if one was returned) so the server-tool loop can continue.
Raise max_tokens and resend the original request.
questions.explanation: pause_turn means a server-tool loop hit its iteration limit, so the turn is incomplete. You resume by passing the assistant content back unchanged. It is never produced by client tool_use, so there is no local tool to run.
rationales: The turn is unfinished; returning now drops work.
Server tools run on Anthropic's side; there is nothing to execute locally.
That is the max_tokens remedy, not pause_turn.

questions.stem: An Agent SDK job is configured with max_turns=30 and max_budget_usd=5. The final ResultMessage has subtype "error_max_budget_usd". Which statement is accurate?
options: The run succeeded; read the answer from the result field as usual.
The budget backstop stopped the run; there is no result field, but total_cost_usd, usage, num_turns and session_id are still reported.
The SDK guarantees spend never exceeded exactly $5.00.
The error means the API key ran out of credits.
questions.explanation: Only the success subtype carries result, while every subtype reports cost, usage, turn count and session_id. Spend can overshoot max_budget_usd by up to one response, so the cap is a backstop rather than an exact limit.
rationales: result is present only on success.
Spend can overshoot by up to one response.
It reflects the configured run budget, not account credit.

questions.stem: A long-running Agent SDK session starts ignoring a rule ("never touch files under /infra") that was stated only in the first user prompt. Logs show a compact_boundary system message shortly before the violations. What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Repeat the rule in uppercase in the first prompt.
Disable compaction so the original prompt is never summarised.
Move the rule into CLAUDE.md loaded via settingSources (re-injected every request), and enforce it with a hook or permission rule as well.
Switch to a larger model.
questions.explanation: Compaction summarises earlier conversation, so details in the initial prompt can be lost. Persistent rules belong in CLAUDE.md, which is re-injected each request, and hard constraints are best backed by enforcement such as a PreToolUse hook or permission rules.
rationales: Emphasis does not survive summarisation any better.
Compaction is what keeps long sessions inside the context window.
Model size does not fix lost context.

questions.stem: Which statements about the Claude Agent SDK's controls are accurate? (Select two.)
options: disallowed_tools blocks the listed tools regardless of other settings.
allowed_tools removes every tool not on the list from the agent.
max_turns and max_budget_usd default to no limit, so you should set them explicitly.
bypassPermissions is the recommended mode for production hosts.
questions.explanation: disallowed_tools is the blocking control, and both loop backstops default to unlimited. allowed_tools only auto-approves its tools while unlisted tools remain available, and bypassPermissions belongs only in an isolated sandbox.
rationales: It auto-approves; it does not remove other tools.
Only appropriate inside an isolated sandbox.

questions.stem: After returning tool results, the bot sometimes gets an end_turn with only two or three tokens of output. The code sends each user message as [tool_result, tool_result, {type: 'text', text: 'Here are the results, please continue.'}]. Which actions follow the documented guidance? (Select two.)
options: Stop appending free text after the tool_result blocks in that user message.
Retry the identical request until a longer answer appears.
If the problem persists, append a new user message such as "Please continue" as a last resort.
Force tool_choice to "any" on the next call.
questions.explanation: An almost empty end_turn usually comes from adding text right after tool_result blocks, and retrying unchanged does not help. Fix the message shape first, and as a last resort send a new user message asking the model to continue.
rationales: The same input tends to produce the same empty turn.
Forcing a tool call does not fix the cause, and forced tool_choice ("any"/"tool") is not supported on some current models.

questions.stem: A team starts a new agent project by adopting a heavy agent framework whose abstractions hide the exact prompts and API responses. Debugging failures has become slow. What does Anthropic's 'Building effective agents' guidance recommend?
options: Add a second framework for observability.
Start with the LLM APIs directly (many patterns are a few lines of code), and if you use a framework, make sure you understand the underlying code.
Replace tools with longer system prompts.
Use voting parallelization to mask failures.
questions.explanation: The guidance suggests starting with the LLM APIs directly because frameworks add abstraction that can obscure prompts and responses. Transparency into what the model sees and returns is essential for debugging agents.
rationales: Doesn't address transparency and removes capabilities.
Voting doesn't explain failures and multiplies cost.

questions.stem: A document-QA agent built on the Client SDK stops with stop_reason "model_context_window_exceeded" after many retrieval tool calls. What is the right interpretation and response?
options: The answer is complete; return it.
Treat the response as truncated, and reduce what is in context (for example clear or summarise old tool results, or delegate retrieval to a subagent that returns a summary).
Raise max_tokens and resend the same history.
Switch the loop to check for the word DONE instead.
questions.explanation: model_context_window_exceeded means the context window is full and the output should be treated as truncated. The fix is to shrink the context, for example by clearing old tool results or isolating noisy work in a subagent, rather than just raising output limits.
rationales: Raising max_tokens doesn't free context space.
Text sentinels are a fragile substitute for stop_reason.

questions.stem:
A developer migrating from another LLM provider sends this request and gets a 400 invalid_request_error. What is the most likely cause?

```json
{"model": "claude-opus-5-5", "max_tokens": 512,
 "messages": [{"role": "system", "content": "You are helpful."},
              {"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}]}
```
options: The messages array contains a 'system' role; the system prompt must be the top-level system parameter.
max_tokens is too small for the model.
The model ID must be passed as a header, not in the body.
The content fields must be arrays of blocks, not strings.
questions.explanation: The system prompt belongs in the top-level system parameter, and the messages array must start with a user turn. Newer models accept a system-role message only mid-conversation, after a user turn.
rationales: Correct: a system message cannot open the messages array; use the top-level system parameter.
model is a required body field.
Strings are an accepted shorthand for a single text block.

questions.stem: Which three fields are required in every Messages API request body?
options: model, messages, system
model, max_tokens, messages
model, messages, temperature
messages, max_tokens, stream
questions.explanation: model, max_tokens and messages are required. system, temperature and stream are optional.
rationales: temperature is not required, and it is not even supported on current models.
model is required; stream is optional.

questions.stem: Users report that answers in the support chat sometimes end mid-sentence. Logs show those responses have stop_reason "max_tokens". What is the best fix?
options: Retry the identical request with exponential backoff.
Ask the model to "be brief" only on retries.
Increase max_tokens appropriately and/or instruct the model to be concise, and handle max_tokens explicitly in code.
Add a stop sequence so the model stops at the end of a sentence.
questions.explanation: max_tokens means the output hit your cap and was truncated. Raise the cap to fit realistic answers, prompt for concision, and detect the stop reason to continue or warn.
rationales: It is not an error; the same request will truncate again.
Changing behaviour only on retry still lets the first answer truncate, and nothing handles the stop reason.
A stop sequence would make responses end earlier, not prevent truncation.

questions.stem: A user asks a follow-up question in your chat app, but Claude responds as if it has never seen the earlier conversation. The code sends only the latest user message. Why?
options: Prompt caching expired after 5 minutes.
The API key changed between requests.
The conversation exceeded the context window.
The Messages API is stateless; prior turns must be included in every request.
questions.explanation: Claude has no memory between API calls. The application must resend the relevant conversation history in messages each time.
rationales: Caching never stores conversation state on your behalf; it only discounts identical prefixes you send.
Only the latest message was sent, so the window isn't the issue.

questions.stem: During a traffic spike your service receives HTTP 429 responses with a retry-after header. What should the client do?
options: Wait at least the retry-after duration, then retry with exponential backoff and jitter.
Immediately retry in a tight loop until it succeeds.
Switch to a new API key for each request.
Treat it as a permanent failure and return an error to the user.
questions.explanation: 429 is a rate_limit_error. Honour retry-after, back off exponentially with jitter, and smooth or queue traffic.
rationales: Tight loops worsen the rate-limit problem.
Rotating keys to dodge limits is not a valid strategy; back off and smooth traffic instead.
A 429 that carries retry-after is transient and retryable.

questions.stem: Which of these errors should your retry logic retry automatically? (Select two.)
options: 400 invalid_request_error
529 overloaded_error
401 authentication_error
500 api_error
questions.explanation: 5xx errors such as 500 api_error and 529 overloaded_error are transient server-side conditions; retry them with backoff (the SDKs already retry them twice by default). 400 and 401 indicate problems with the request or key that a retry will not fix.
rationales: A malformed request will fail again; fix the code.
A bad key won't become valid on retry.

questions.stem: Why should exponential backoff include random jitter?
options: It makes the total retry time shorter.
The API requires a random delay before accepting retries.
It spreads retries from many clients so they don't hit the API simultaneously.
It changes the request so it is not treated as a duplicate.
questions.explanation: Without jitter, many clients that failed at the same moment retry in lock-step (thundering herd), recreating the overload.
rationales: Jitter adds a little delay; its goal isn't speed.

questions.stem: When streaming a response, in which server-sent event will you find the final stop_reason?
options: message_start
content_block_stop
message_stop
message_delta
questions.explanation: message_delta carries top-level changes to the message, including stop_reason and cumulative output token usage. message_stop then signals the end of the stream.
rationales: message_start has the initial message shell; stop_reason is null there.
message_stop marks the end but doesn't carry stop_reason.

questions.stem: Your streaming handler throws a JSON parse error when Claude calls a tool. It calls JSON.parse() on every content_block_delta of type input_json_delta. What is the fix?
options: Accumulate the partial_json strings for the block and parse once at content_block_stop (or use the SDK's stream helpers).
Set tool_choice to none while streaming.
Ask Claude in the system prompt to emit complete JSON in each chunk.
Disable streaming whenever tools are provided.
questions.explanation: input_json_delta events contain fragments of the tool input JSON. Concatenate them and parse when the block is complete; SDK helpers like finalMessage() do this for you.
rationales: That would prevent tool use entirely.
Chunking is a transport detail the model doesn't control.
Streaming works with tools; this is unnecessary.

questions.stem: Which statements about streaming with the Messages API are true? (Select two.)
options: Streaming is only available in the Python SDK.
An error event (e.g. overloaded_error) can arrive after the stream has started with HTTP 200.
Streaming reduces the number of tokens billed.
Streaming is recommended for long outputs; the SDK rejects non-streaming requests expected to run over 10 minutes.
questions.explanation: Errors can be delivered mid-stream as error events, so handlers must cope with them. Streaming (or batching) is the documented path for long requests, and it also improves perceived latency.
rationales: Both Python and TypeScript SDKs (and raw HTTP) support streaming.
Streaming changes how tokens are delivered, not how many are generated.

questions.stem: A response comes back with content blocks [thinking, text]. The code prints resp.content[0].text and crashes. What's the right pattern?
options: Use resp.text, which concatenates all blocks.
Set max_tokens higher so text comes first.
Iterate over resp.content and handle blocks by their type.
Ask the model in the system prompt to always put text first.
questions.explanation: Responses can contain several block types (thinking, text, tool_use). Code should iterate and filter by type rather than assume the first block is text.
rationales: There is no documented field that concatenates blocks; read the content array by block type.
Block order doesn't depend on max_tokens.
Block order is not something to control by prompt, and tool_use blocks would still break the code.

questions.stem: Legal users need every claim in an answer to point to the exact passage in an uploaded contract PDF. What should the developer do?
options: Convert the PDF to an image and ask Claude to describe it.
Ask Claude to put quotes in bold and trust them.
Ask Claude to wrap every quote in <quote> tags and trust them as verbatim.
Send the PDF as a document block with citations enabled, and render the returned citation spans.
questions.explanation: The citations feature returns structured references to exact spans/pages of the provided documents, which is far more reliable than free-text quoting.
rationales: This loses text fidelity and still doesn't produce citations.
Free-text quotes can be paraphrased or fabricated.
Tagged free-text quotes can still be paraphrased or invented; only citations give structured references to source spans.

questions.stem: How should a PDF be sent to Claude through the Messages API?
options: As a document content block with a base64, URL or file-id source.
As an image block with media_type application/pdf.
As a system prompt attachment.
As a text block containing the base64 string.
questions.explanation: PDFs use document content blocks. Claude processes both text and visual elements of the pages.
rationales: Image blocks are for image media types.
Raw base64 in a text block is just meaningless text to the model.

questions.stem: In a vision prompt with one large screenshot and a detailed question, which layout typically works best?
options: Image in the system prompt, question in the user turn.
Image first, then the question in the same user message.
Send the image and question in two separate API calls.
Question first, then the image.
questions.explanation: Placing images (and documents) before the text instructions generally yields better results.
rationales: Images belong in user message content.
Separate calls lose context because the API is stateless.
It works but is generally less effective.

questions.stem: Long support conversations are getting slow and expensive because every turn resends the whole history. Which approaches are appropriate? (Select two.)
options: Put the stable prefix (system prompt, policy docs) under prompt caching.
Move the conversation history into the system prompt to make it free.
Summarise older turns into a compact summary and keep recent turns verbatim.
Rely on the API to remember earlier turns server-side.
questions.explanation: Summarising/trimming reduces input tokens, and caching the stable prefix makes repeated content cheaper and faster.
rationales: System prompt tokens are billed like any other input tokens.

questions.stem: Your team hard-codes the model ID and prompt text in 14 different files. A developer updated the model ID in some files but not others, and production now gives inconsistent answers across endpoints. What is the best configuration practice going forward?
options: Copy the prompt into each file's comments for documentation.
Store prompts in the database without version history so they can be edited live.
Have each service choose the newest model at start-up so they all stay current.
Centralise the model ID, parameters and versioned prompts in per-environment config, pin one model ID, and change it only after running evals.
questions.explanation: A single pinned model ID and versioned prompts in config make behaviour consistent and changes deliberate and testable. Every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot, so behaviour changes only when the ID changes, and that change should pass evals.
rationales: Unversioned live edits make regressions untraceable.
Automatic model changes make behaviour change without review or evals.

questions.stem: What should you log with every Claude API call in production to support debugging and audits? (Select three.)
options: The request-id returned by the API
The model ID and prompt version used
The full API key
usage (input/output/cache tokens) and stop_reason
questions.explanation: request-id enables support investigations, model/prompt version enables regression tracing, and usage/stop_reason enables cost tracking and failure detection. Never log secrets.
rationales: Logging secrets is a security risk.

questions.stem: Before building the invoice extraction feature, the PM says 'it should be accurate'. What is the best next step?
options: Add "be accurate" to the system prompt so accuracy is covered.
Define measurable success criteria (e.g. field-level accuracy on a labelled test set, cost per document, latency) and build an eval set.
Pick the largest model to maximise accuracy.
Start coding the prompt and see how it goes.
questions.explanation: Specific, measurable success criteria turn a vague goal into something testable and guide model, prompt and cost decisions.
rationales: An instruction is not a measurable criterion; you still cannot tell whether the feature is good enough.
Model choice should follow evaluation against criteria.
Without criteria you can't tell if iterations help.

questions.stem: A request returns 400 with a message saying tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after. What happened?
options: The model doesn't support tool use.
tool_choice was set to auto.
The next user message after the assistant's tool_use didn't contain matching tool_result blocks (e.g. it contained only text, or results were placed in a later message).
The tool's input_schema was invalid JSON Schema.
questions.explanation: Every tool_use block must be answered by a tool_result with the matching tool_use_id in the immediately following user message, with tool_result blocks first.
rationales: A bad schema produces a different validation error at definition time.

questions.stem: Which HTTP status indicates the API key is missing or invalid?
questions.explanation: 401 authentication_error means the key is missing, invalid or expired. 403 means the authenticated key lacks permission for the resource.

questions.stem: A request using model ID "claude-sonet-x" (typo) fails. Which error type would you expect?
options: not_found_error (404)
rate_limit_error (429)
api_error (500)
529 overloaded_error
questions.explanation: An unknown model or endpoint results in a not_found_error; it is a client mistake, not something to retry.

questions.stem: After the team switches to anthropic-version 2026-10-21, every request from a summarisation service fails with 400. The payload includes `"temperature": 0.2` copied from old code. What is the best fix?
options: Change temperature to 1.0, its default value.
Remove temperature (and any top_p/top_k) from the request and config, and get consistency from the prompt and structured outputs.
Move temperature into output_config.
Add an anthropic-beta header to re-enable sampling parameters.
questions.explanation: Under API version 2026-10-21, temperature, top_p and top_k return 400 on every model, even at default values, and current models do not support them under the old version either. Remove them and rely on prompts, examples and structured outputs for consistency.
rationales: They return 400 even at default values under 2026-10-21.
output_config holds effort and format, not sampling parameters.
No beta header restores sampling parameters.

questions.stem: Legacy code forces JSON by ending the request with an assistant turn containing "{". After moving to a current Claude model, the request fails with "This model does not support assistant message prefill." What is the best replacement?
options: Prefill "[" instead of "{".
Add a stop sequence of "}" so output ends with valid JSON.
Use structured outputs: output_config.format with a JSON schema.
Put the "{" at the end of the system prompt.
questions.explanation: Prefill is unsupported from Claude 4.6 onward, so any assistant-turn prefill returns 400. Structured outputs (output_config.format with a json_schema) is the supported way to get schema-conforming JSON.
rationales: Any prefill is rejected, whatever the character.
A stop sequence ends generation early and would cut off nested objects; it does not force a format.
This does not guarantee format and is not how output is constrained.

questions.stem: The web front-end currently sends the full conversation history to your backend on every turn, and the backend forwards it to Claude. A security review flags this. Why, and what's better?
options: It wastes bandwidth only; compress it with gzip.
Claude rejects histories created by browsers.
It's fine as long as you use HTTPS.
Clients could tamper with history (e.g. inject fake assistant turns); store history server-side keyed by conversation ID.
questions.explanation: Client-supplied history can be forged to inject instructions or fake prior approvals. Persist authoritative history on the server.
rationales: The API can't tell where history came from.
HTTPS protects transport, not integrity against the user themselves.

questions.stem: Which approach is best when the same 40-page PDF is referenced across hundreds of requests over the day?
options: Upload it once (e.g. Files API) and reference it by id, and use prompt caching for the repeated prefix.
Base64-encode it into every request and increase max_tokens.
Paste its text into the user's question each time with no caching.
Split it into images, one per request.
questions.explanation: Referencing an uploaded file avoids resending large payloads, and caching the document prefix cuts cost and latency on repeated use.
rationales: Works but wastes bandwidth and cost; max_tokens is unrelated.

questions.stem: A stop_reason of "pause_turn" is returned while Claude is using the server-side web search tool. What should the application do?
options: Treat it as an error and retry from scratch.
Send the response content back as the assistant turn in a new request so Claude can continue.
Return the partial answer to the user as final.
Raise max_tokens and send the original request again.
questions.explanation: pause_turn means a server-tool loop hit its iteration limit (10 by default). Send the assistant content back as-is, plus any container id, so Claude resumes where it left off.
rationales: Restarting wastes work and may pause again.
pause_turn is not truncation; restarting discards the paused work.

questions.stem: Which header must accompany every direct HTTP request to the Messages API, besides the API key and content type?
options: anthropic-model
anthropic-beta
anthropic-version
x-request-id
questions.explanation: anthropic-version is required; the current version is 2026-10-21 (previously 2023-06-01). anthropic-beta is only for opting into beta features.

questions.stem: Your application lets the model's output be inserted directly into an internal web dashboard as HTML. What is the main risk and mitigation?
options: Latency; stream the output.
Token waste; ask for shorter output.
Copyright; add a disclaimer.
Cross-site scripting from untrusted model output (possibly induced by injected content); escape/sanitise output before rendering.
questions.explanation: Model output must be treated as untrusted input. Escape or sanitise it before rendering to prevent XSS.

questions.stem: A TypeScript service sets `maxRetries: 0` on the client and implements its own retry wrapper that retries every thrown error 5 times with a fixed 1-second delay. What are the problems? (Select two.)
options: It retries non-retryable errors like 400 and 401.
Fixed delays without jitter can synchronise retries and prolong overload.
The SDK forbids custom retry logic.
Retries always double the token cost even on failure.
questions.explanation: Retry only transient errors (429, 5xx/529, connection errors) and use exponential backoff with jitter.
rationales: This is not a defined rule; the real defects are what gets retried and how it is spaced (and the custom layer also replaced the SDK's sensible defaults).

questions.stem: A product owner asks for a support assistant that is "fast, cheap and good". Which set of success criteria is the best starting point?
options: "Users should like it" and "it should feel quick".
Zero incorrect answers on any input.
Use the most capable model available and the longest system prompt allowed.
≥90% of answers rated correct on a 300-ticket labelled set, p95 time-to-first-token under 1.5 s, and average cost per conversation under a set ceiling.
questions.explanation: Good success criteria are specific, measurable and achievable, and they map directly onto an eval set and production metrics. Vague, solution-shaped or impossible targets cannot guide model or prompt decisions.
rationales: Not measurable; you cannot tell when you have met it.
Unachievable for any probabilistic system; it blocks shipping without guiding improvement.
That is a solution choice, not a success criterion.
Correct: each criterion is specific and testable.

questions.stem: Extraction accuracy passes its criterion, but p95 latency is double the target. The team has spent two weeks shortening the prompt with little effect. What should they try next?
options: Add "respond as fast as possible" to the system prompt.
Remove the eval set to save time per iteration.
Raise max_tokens so responses are not truncated.
Evaluate a faster model and/or a lower effort level against the same eval set, keeping the change only if accuracy still passes.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's prompt-engineering guidance notes that some criteria, such as latency and cost, are better met by choosing a different model than by prompting. Effort is also a strong lever, and the eval set confirms that accuracy holds.
rationales: Instructions do not reliably change generation speed.
Without evals you cannot tell whether a faster setup still meets the accuracy bar.
max_tokens is a cap; raising it does not reduce latency.

questions.stem: Which of these are well-formed success criteria for an LLM feature? (Select two.)
options: The classifier assigns the correct category to at least 92% of a 500-ticket held-out set.
The model should understand the customer.
Fewer than 1% of responses in a weekly sample of 200 contain a policy violation, as judged by the review rubric.
Use XML tags in the prompt.
questions.explanation: Success criteria state a measurable outcome and how it is measured. "Understand the customer" is vague, and "use XML tags" is an implementation technique, not a criterion.
rationales: Correct: specific, measurable, with a defined test set.
Correct: a measurable rate with a defined sample and rubric.
A prompting technique, not an outcome.

questions.stem: A newer Claude model is released. Your production config pins an older model ID. What is the best way to adopt the new one?
options: Change the ID in production right away; newer models are always better for every task.
Wait until users complain about quality before considering it.
Run your eval suite against the new model ID, compare quality, latency and cost, then roll it out behind a flag (shadow or canary) with a rollback path.
Point production at a gateway alias that always resolves to the newest model.
questions.explanation: Model changes are behaviour changes. Evaluate against your criteria first, then release in stages with a quick rollback; parameter support and tokenization can differ between generations.
rationales: Newer is not automatically better for your task, and unsupported parameters can break requests.
Reactive and slow; it ignores possible gains and risks.
A moving alias brings in untested behaviour changes.

questions.stem: A team is defining what to monitor after launching a Claude-backed feature. Which signals give the most direct early warning of quality or reliability problems? (Select two.)
options: The distribution of stop_reason values, especially rising max_tokens, refusal or model_context_window_exceeded rates.
The number of lines of code in the prompt template.
Scores on a regularly sampled set of live outputs graded against the same rubric as the eval set.
The number of developers with access to the API key.
questions.explanation: A shifting stop_reason mix shows truncation, refusals or context pressure, and sampled grading against the eval rubric tracks real-world quality. Prompt length and key access are not quality signals (key access is a security concern).
rationales: Not a quality or reliability signal.
A security-hygiene concern, not a quality signal.

questions.stem: A prompt tweak fixed one escalated complaint, went straight to production, and broke refund-related answers for two days before anyone noticed. Which process change prevents this best?
options: Version prompts, run the eval suite (with refund cases) in CI as a gate on every prompt change, and release behind a flag that allows instant rollback.
Only allow senior engineers to edit prompts.
Freeze the prompt permanently.
Lower max_tokens so that changes have less effect.
questions.explanation: Treat prompts as code: versioned, tested against evals before release, and rolled out in a way that can be reversed quickly. Production failures should also become new eval cases.
rationales: Stops improvement rather than making change safe.
Unrelated to regressions and risks truncation.

questions.stem: You want to see how a new prompt-and-model combination behaves on real traffic without any user seeing its output. Which release technique fits?
options: Canary release to 5% of users
Shadow mode: run the new version in parallel on live inputs, log and grade its outputs, but serve the current version
Blue/green switch of all traffic at once
A/B test with users choosing the version
questions.explanation: Shadow mode exercises the new version on real inputs while users keep receiving the current version, so you can compare without user impact. Canary and A/B tests expose some users to the new output.
rationales: Some users see the new output.
All users switch at once, with no comparison step.

questions.stem: An agent has an issue_refund tool. After a network timeout, the service retried the tool execution and the customer was refunded twice. What is the best fix?
options: Set maxRetries to 0 on the Anthropic client.
Tell the model in the system prompt never to call issue_refund twice.
Make the refund idempotent: key it on a stable ID (e.g. the order ID or the tool_use id), record the key with the refund, and on a repeat return the stored result instead of refunding again.
Increase the HTTP timeout so timeouts never happen.
questions.explanation: Timeouts are ambiguous: the side effect may have happened even though the caller saw a failure. Retries exist at several layers, so the side-effecting operation itself must be idempotent, with a check-then-act on a stable key.
rationales: The duplicate came from tool execution, not the Claude API call; and disabling retries removes resilience without fixing the root cause.
Prompts cannot guarantee exactly-once execution, and the retry here was in your code.
Timeouts can still occur; a longer timeout only makes them rarer.

questions.stem: A nightly job submits 40,000 classification requests via the Message Batches API and writes results back by array position. Some documents end up with another document's label. Why?
options: The batch was too large and was silently truncated.
Batch results can come back in any order; results must be matched to inputs by custom_id.
Batches round labels to the most common category.
Prompt caching mixed up the documents.
questions.explanation: Batch results are not guaranteed to follow submission order. Give each request a unique custom_id (such as the document ID) and join results on it.
rationales: 40,000 is within the per-batch request limit, and nothing is silently truncated.
Caching reuses identical prefixes; it does not swap outputs between requests.

questions.stem: The batch-submitting worker crashed halfway through a backfill and the scheduler will re-run it. How do you avoid paying twice and writing duplicate rows?
options: Use random UUIDs as custom_id so every run is unique.
Always re-submit everything; batches are cheap.
Use a deterministic custom_id per document (e.g. the document ID), record which IDs already have stored results or are in an active batch, submit only the rest, and upsert results keyed by that ID.
Set stream: true on each batch request to see progress.
questions.explanation: A deterministic key makes the job idempotent: re-runs skip completed work and writes become upserts. custom_id must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$, so derive it from a stable identifier that fits.
rationales: Random IDs make it impossible to recognise work already done.
Batches cost 50% of normal, not nothing, and duplicate rows still appear.
stream: true is not allowed in batch requests.

questions.stem: A service asks for very long reports with a large max_tokens on a non-streaming call. The SDK refuses the request before sending it, warning that it may take longer than 10 minutes. What is the best fix?
options: Stream the response (or move the job to the Message Batches API if nobody is waiting).
Disable the SDK and send the request with raw HTTP and a one-hour socket timeout.
Split the report into 50 separate non-streaming calls with tiny max_tokens.
Lower max_tokens to 256.
questions.explanation: Long requests belong on streaming or the Batches API; the SDK rejects non-streaming requests expected to exceed 10 minutes. Streaming also gives users output sooner.
rationales: Works around a safeguard and stays fragile against network idle timeouts.
Adds complexity and loses coherence; the documented path is streaming or batches.

questions.stem: A request fails with HTTP 504 timeout_error. What is the most appropriate handling?
options: Treat it as a client bug and never retry.
Rotate the API key.
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, keeping any side effects idempotent; if it recurs, reduce the work per request or use streaming.
Retry immediately in a tight loop until it succeeds.
questions.explanation: 504 timeout_error is a server-side timeout and is transient, so backoff retries are appropriate. Because the work may have partly completed, keep the surrounding operations idempotent.
rationales: Tight loops add load and ignore backoff.

questions.stem: Error-handling code checks `if 'overloaded' in str(err)` to decide whether to retry, and production incidents are hard to trace with Anthropic support. What should change?
options: Log the full API key with each error so support can find the account.
Catch the SDK's typed exception classes for the retry decision and log the request id (request-id / _request_id) with each failure.
Retry every exception, regardless of type, five times.
Lower max_tokens to reduce errors.
questions.explanation: Typed exceptions are a stable contract while message text can change, and the request id lets support find the exact request. Never log secrets.
rationales: Retries non-retryable errors such as 400 and 401.
Unrelated to error classification or traceability.

questions.stem: A service has received 429 rate_limit_error responses for an hour. The responses carry no retry-after header, and backoff retries keep failing. What is the most likely cause and response?
options: A transient overload; keep retrying with longer backoff.
An invalid API key; rotate it.
A malformed request; fix the JSON.
A tier spend cap was reached; retries will not help, so alert an owner to raise the limit or change plan, and degrade gracefully meanwhile.
questions.explanation: A 429 caused by a tier spend cap carries no retry-after and keeps failing until the limit changes. Ordinary rate-limit 429s are transient and include retry-after guidance.
rationales: This 429 will not clear by waiting minutes.

questions.stem: A long-running research chat occasionally returns stop_reason "model_context_window_exceeded". How should the application respond?
options: Treat the response as truncated, then shrink the context (summarise or compact older turns, drop stale tool results) before continuing.
Show the response as complete; that stop reason is informational only.
Retry the identical request with backoff.
Switch on a lower temperature.
questions.explanation: model_context_window_exceeded means generation stopped because the context filled, so the output is truncated. Reduce the context through trimming, summarisation or compaction before the next call.
rationales: The same context will hit the same limit.
Sampling parameters are not supported on current models and do not affect context size.

questions.stem: Monitoring shows some responses arrive as HTTP 200 but the chat displays nothing useful. Their stop_reason is "refusal". What is the recommended handling?
options: Treat HTTP 200 as success and display whatever content exists.
Branch on stop_reason, read stop_details to understand the refusal, then retry on a configured fallback model or show a graceful message, and log it.
Retry the identical request on the same model until it succeeds.
Convert the refusal into a 500 and let the SDK retry it.
questions.explanation: A refusal comes back as HTTP 200 with stop_reason "refusal" and is billed. The documented handling is to read stop_details and retry on a fallback model where appropriate, otherwise surface a safe message.
rationales: A 200 is not proof of a usable answer.
The same request on the same model is likely to be refused again.
Re-labelling it causes pointless retries of the same request.

questions.stem: A team runs dev, staging and prod for a Claude-backed service. Which configuration approach is best?
options: One codebase; per-environment config for model ID, limits, prompt version and flags; credentials per environment (service-account keys or Workload Identity Federation) loaded from a secrets manager.
Commit each environment's API key to its own config file in the repo.
Share one developer's personal API key across all environments.
Maintain a separate code branch per environment with hard-coded values.
questions.explanation: Environment-specific values belong in config, and secrets belong in a secrets manager, with workload identities rather than personal keys. Personal keys stop working when their owner is removed, and committed keys leak.
rationales: Keys must never be committed to source control.
Identity-backed personal keys break when the owner leaves and blur audit trails.
Branch-per-environment drifts and makes releases untestable.

questions.stem: Quality dropped last Tuesday, and nobody can tell which prompt or model produced the bad extractions. What should the team put in place? (Select two.)
options: Store prompts as versioned artifacts (git or a prompt registry) with a version identifier.
Log the prompt version, model ID and request id with every output.
Let operators edit the live prompt in a database field without history.
Use a random model per request to spread risk.
questions.explanation: Versioned prompts plus per-output logging of prompt version, model and request id make regressions traceable and reversible. Unversioned live edits and random model choice destroy that traceability.
rationales: Changes become untraceable and impossible to roll back.

questions.stem: A streamed response starts with HTTP 200, sends some text, then delivers an error event of type overloaded_error. What should the client do?
options: Ignore it; an HTTP 200 stream cannot fail.
Treat it as a permanent 400-class failure.
Append the partial text to history as a complete assistant turn.
Treat it like a 529: discard or mark the partial output, then retry with backoff (or fall back), and tell the user if it persists.
questions.explanation: Errors can arrive mid-stream after the 200; overloaded_error corresponds to HTTP 529. Handle it as a transient failure, and do not store the partial output as a finished turn.
rationales: Overload is transient, not a client bug.
Storing a truncated turn as complete corrupts history.

questions.stem: You are designing a nightly job that classifies 60,000 support tickets; nobody waits on the results. Which design choices are correct? (Select two.)
options: Use the Message Batches API for the 50% discount, with each ticket ID as custom_id.
Set stream: true on every batch request to receive results faster.
After the batch ends, check for errored and expired results and re-submit those in a new batch.
Assume every request was valid because the batch submission was accepted.
questions.explanation: Batches suit offline work at half the cost, and custom_id joins results to tickets. Params are validated when the batch ends, so errored (and expired) results must be checked and re-queued; streaming is not allowed in batches.
rationales: stream: true is not allowed in a batch.
Validation happens when the batch ends; invalid requests appear as errored results.

questions.stem: A CI job runs `claude "review the diff"` and hangs until the job times out. What's the fix?
options: Use claude -p "review the diff" (print/headless mode), optionally with --output-format json.
Increase the CI timeout.
Run claude in a Docker container.
Add --verbose.
questions.explanation: Without -p, Claude Code starts an interactive session waiting for input. -p processes the prompt, prints the result and exits.

questions.stem: Your team wants shared Claude Code permission rules committed to the repo, while each developer can keep personal overrides out of git. Which files?
options: .mcp.json and .env
.claude/settings.json (shared) and .claude/settings.local.json (personal, git-ignored)
CLAUDE.md for both
~/.claude/settings.json for both
questions.explanation: Project settings.json is shared via version control; settings.local.json holds personal, uncommitted settings.
rationales: CLAUDE.md is memory/instructions, not permissions config.
User-level settings aren't shared with the team.
